plan.topic: Sick on tirzepatide (flu, cold or stomach bug): why vomiting or diarrhoea can lead to dehydration, the label's kidney warning, and when to call your prescriber
plan.angle: Open: 'Got a stomach bug on tirzepatide? The thing to watch is fluids. The label notes rare reports of sudden kidney injury, mostly in people who became dehydrated from vomiting, diarrhoea or nausea.' New fact: what the label says (the reports, sometimes in people with no known kidney disease, and that prescribers may check kidney function). Dehydration signs come from NHS and are tagged NHS: feeling thirsty, dark yellow strong-smelling pee, peeing less, dizziness, tiredness. Untagged tips: sip fluids through the day unless you've been told to limit fluids; ask a pharmacist before taking cold or flu remedies. If you have diabetes and use insulin or a sulfonylurea, ask your prescriber for a sick-day plan. Red flags: vomiting or diarrhoea you can't keep up with, very little urine, or dizziness means contacting your prescriber or healthcare provider right away. Then 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own; ask your prescriber what to do on sick days', the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. No dosing or skip-a-dose content.
plan.working_title: Sick on Tirzepatide? Why Fluids Matter More
plan.why: Flu season is starting and competition is low. The calm 'is this normal?' body-worry format is our proven top Short. It also tests demand for the dehydration Lane A long-form on the ship list. | fact-check: I checked the current Zepbound label (revised 8/2026, uspl.lilly.com). Section 5 is titled 'Acute Kidney Injury Due to Volume Depletion'. It reports postmarketing acute kidney injury, mostly in people whose nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea led to dehydration, some without known kidney disease. It tells clinicians to monitor kidney function. The label does NOT list dehydration signs, so the angle's 'new fact: the dehydration signs it lists' would credit the label with something it doesn't say. Take the signs from NHS (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dehydration/) and tag them NHS. The angle's 'linked to kidney problems' is loose. Use the label's own idea: reports of sudden kidney injury, mostly in people who got dehydrated. Leave out 'hemodialysis', which is alarming on its own, and keep the framing calm. Add one plain line for people with diabetes who also take insulin or a sulfonylurea: being ill can affect blood sugar, so ask your prescriber about a sick-day plan. Don't give any instructions for adjusting doses. Keep 'unless you've been told to limit fluids' and the pharmacist line, and leave both untagged.

Vomiting or diarrhoea on tirzepatide can lead to dehydration. The label notes reports of sudden kidney injury, mostly in people dehydrated by nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Here's what helps and when to contact your prescriber.

Don't stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

social.instagram_caption:
Vomiting or diarrhoea on tirzepatide? Miserable, I know. Watch your fluids.

Here's why: the label notes reports of sudden kidney injury, mostly in people dehydrated by nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. It tells prescribers to monitor kidney function in people with these side effects, especially when starting or increasing the dose.

NHS signs of dehydration to watch for:
• Thirst, dark yellow, strong-smelling pee
• Peeing less than usual
• Dizziness or tiredness

What can help:
• Small sips, building up gradually (unless you've been told to limit fluids)
• Ask a pharmacist about rehydration sachets
• On insulin or a sulfonylurea? Ask your prescriber for a sick-day plan

Can't keep up with vomiting or diarrhoea, very little pee, or dizziness that doesn't go away? Contact your prescriber or healthcare provider right away. Confused, very drowsy or struggling to breathe? Get emergency help right away.

Don't stop or change your medicines on your own — ask your prescriber what to do on sick days.

factcheck.summary: The content is accurate and safe. Both sources exist, are reachable and say what the script claims. I checked the Zepbound label (revised 8/2026), section 5.3 "Acute Kidney Injury Due to Volume Depletion". It says "the majority of the reported events occurred in patients who experienced gastrointestinal adverse reactions leading to dehydration such as nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea". It also says to monitor kidney function "especially during dosage initiation and escalation". The NHS Dehydration page (last reviewed 1 May 2026) supports the list of signs, the advice to start with small sips, the pharmacist's oral rehydration solutions, and the 999 signs (confusion, being very sleepy, trouble breathing). The safety lines are all there: the limit-fluids caveat, the sick-day plan for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, the don't-stop line, "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line, and the urgency words "right away". There are no dosing or titration instructions and no shaming. Three small wording fixes would match the sources more exactly.

issues.claim: The label tells prescribers to monitor kidney function in people with these side effects, especially early in treatment.
issues.problem: The label says "especially during dosage initiation and escalation". "Early in treatment" leaves out dose increases, which narrows what the label says. Describing when the label asks for monitoring isn't a dosing instruction.
issues.fix: The label tells prescribers to monitor kidney function in people with these side effects, especially when starting or increasing the dose.

issues.claim: ...very little pee, or dizziness? Contact your prescriber or healthcare provider right away.
issues.problem: The NHS 'get help urgently' tier says dizziness "that does not go away" when standing, not any dizziness. A bare "dizziness" makes the urgent tier broader than the source.
issues.fix: Narration: "Can't keep up with vomiting or diarrhoea, very little pee, or dizziness that doesn't go away? Contact your prescriber or healthcare provider right away. Confused, very drowsy or struggling to breathe? Get emergency help right away." List item 3: "Dizziness that doesn't go away". Optionally add source_ids ["s2"] to scene 7, since the NHS page supports both tiers.

issues.claim: Small, frequent sips through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids.
issues.problem: The NHS says to start with small sips if you feel sick and then gradually drink more. The 'limit fluids' caveat is our own safety line, but it's tagged to s2 together with the NHS advice. Craft notes say our own caveats carry no source tag.
issues.fix: Narration: "What helps? Start with small sips, then gradually drink more. Unless you've been told to limit fluids. A pharmacist can suggest rehydration sachets." Keep s2 on the scene for the sips and pharmacist lines only; the limit-fluids line is our own caveat and isn't attributed to the NHS.
